Two leaflet-worthy consequences fall straight out of the analogy. Antibiotics do nothing for viruses, for the same reason weedkiller doesn't fix a fence — a cold isn't a weed, it's a different category of problem, with no bacterial machinery to attack. And you finish the course for the same reason you don't stop weeding at the first clear patch: the toughest weeds are the last ones alive, and stopping early leaves them in charge of the garden.

Kept simple on purpose: the analogy omits how the immune system does most of the actual clearing, with the drug tipping the balance — a second paragraph's worth of detail, not the first.
What is a stock market index? Explain it so my retired neighbor gets it — she thinks the news is reporting the price of 'the market'.

Give her a shopping basket. Imagine that every week, someone prices the exact same basket of groceries — same bread, same milk, same eggs — and announces how much the basket costs. The number isn't the price of any single item; it's a way to watch the whole shop's prices move with one figure. When the basket gets dearer, groceries in general are getting dearer.

A stock index is that basket, filled with companies instead of groceries. The S&P 500 tracks the same fixed 'basket' of 500 large companies; when the news says 'the index rose 1%', it means the basket as a whole rose — not every company in it, any more than every item in the grocery basket rose when the total did. Some fell while others climbed.

Her confusion is the common one, and the basket fixes it precisely: there is no single thing called 'the market' with a price. There's a standardized basket, repriced constantly, so that change over time means something. Once she has the basket, she'll also ask the right next question — what's in it, and who chose — which is exactly where index literacy starts.
Why does Google show the pages it shows? I'm a plumber with a website — explain it in my terms, not tech terms.

Think about how you get work: recommendations. When a homeowner asks around, the plumber whose name comes up from five different neighbors — especially the neighbors known for good judgment — gets the call. Google ranks pages roughly the way your street ranks plumbers: by who vouches for them. Every link from another website to yours is a neighbor mentioning your name, and mentions from respected, relevant sites count like mentions from the street's most trusted household.

The second half is the van and the shopfront: when someone does call, Google also checks that your page actually answers the question typed — that you say 'emergency plumber in Leeds' if that's the job — the way a customer checks your van has your trade and town on it, not just a phone number.

What this tells you practically: chasing tricks is like paying for fake reviews — it can work briefly and then ruin you when discovered. The durable strategy is the trade strategy: do work worth recommending, earn mentions from real local sites, and make sure your page plainly says what you do and where. The algorithm changes constantly; the reputation logic underneath it has been stable for twenty-five years.
I teach middle school. My students keep confusing computer viruses with biological ones — same word, they think same thing. Help me untangle it for them.

Use their confusion as the lesson: the word is the same because the analogy is old and mostly good — and then show them exactly where it snaps, because that's where understanding lives. What genuinely matches: both are small things that can't reproduce alone; both need a host — a cell, or a computer running a program — to make copies; both spread from host to host; both can be harmless passengers or wreck the host; and 'vaccination' even has an echo in antivirus software that recognizes known threats.

Now the snap. A biological virus is a physical object that evolved over millions of years with no author and no purpose — it isn't trying anything. A computer virus was written, line by line, by a person, for a reason, and it doesn't mutate by accident in the wild the way flu does; its 'evolution' is its author shipping new versions. And the defenses differ in kind: your body fights from inside, learning as it goes, while a computer's defenses are almost entirely an external guard comparing files against a list of known criminals.

End with the general rule, which is worth more than either virus: whenever two things share a name, ask 'who chose this name, and what did they want me to notice — and what does the name hide?' That question will serve them long after the viruses are forgotten.
How do painkillers like ibuprofen work? My kid asked if they 'fix' the injury. Good question, honestly.

Your kid has spotted the exact thing the right analogy clarifies. Use a burglar alarm. When you twist an ankle, the injury is the burglar; the pain is the alarm — a signal, sent to get your attention, that something at the site needs protecting. Ibuprofen doesn't catch the burglar or repair the door. It turns down the alarm's volume at the site itself: it blocks some of the chemical messengers (prostaglandins) that injured tissue uses to raise the alarm and sensitize the area.

That framing answers his real question honestly: no, the painkiller doesn't fix the injury — the ankle heals at its own pace whether or not the alarm is quieter, which is why you can feel fine and still re-injure it by running too soon. The quieter alarm is genuinely useful — it lets you sleep, move gently, function — but it's information being muted, not damage being repaired.

It's also a good place to teach the general skill: for any medicine, ask 'does this treat the cause, the signal, or the symptom downstream of the signal?' — three different jobs, and a lot of confusion clears up once you know which job your pill is doing.
Everyone tells me to diversify my savings but nobody explains what it actually protects against. I'm not putting it all in one stock — what more is there?

Picture an orchard instead of a bank account. A farmer with only apple trees has a magnificent September and a terrifying April: one late frost, one pest that loves apples, and the whole year's income is gone — not because apples are bad, but because every tree shares the same vulnerabilities and the same season. The farmer who plants apples, pears, cherries, and some early and late crops has no single week that can ruin her. Something is always fruiting; a frost that kills the cherry blossom merely dents the year.

That's what diversification actually buys: not higher returns, but the removal of single points of failure. Your savings version: different assets fail in different weather. Shares can fall when the economy sours; cash doesn't fall but quietly loses to inflation; property is solid until you need to sell it quickly. Holding several isn't about finding the winner — nobody knows the winner — it's about making sure no one kind of bad year can take everything.

What the orchard also teaches, and the slogan hides: diversification has limits. A drought hits the whole orchard at once. Some risks are weather for the entire region — a deep recession hurts most assets together — and no planting scheme inside one orchard escapes it. Diversify to survive specific failures, and don't believe it makes you drought-proof.
I've spent $400 and three months on a course I hate and am learning nothing from. Quitting feels like wasting all that. Talk me through it.

Use the cinema version, because it's the same decision with the feelings stripped out. You've paid for a film ticket — that money is gone whether you stay or leave; the cinema will not refund you at the door for your disappointment. The only real question is about the next two hours: are they worth more to you inside this seat, watching a film you're not enjoying, or outside it, doing anything else? The ticket price is not part of that question, because it's identical in both futures.

Your course is the ticket, enlarged. The $400 and three months are spent in every possible future — quitting doesn't waste them any more than staying 'saves' them. What staying actually does is add the next three months to the loss, in order to avoid feeling like the first three were wasted. Economists call the pull you feel the sunk cost fallacy, but you don't need the label: you need the question. If a friend offered you this course today, free, knowing what you now know — would you start it? If not, the only thing keeping you enrolled is a payment that no longer exists.

One honest caveat: 'hating it' and 'it's hard' are different signals. If the course is valuable and merely painful, that's the gym, not the cinema. But if you've genuinely learned that it leads nowhere you want to go, walk out of the film.
I diversified like I was told — different funds, different companies. Then in the crash everything fell together. Was the advice wrong?

The advice was half right, and a truck explains the missing half. Imagine a farmer who learns not to put all her eggs in one basket, so she uses six different baskets — different weaves, different makers, excellent diversification. Then she loads all six into the same truck. On the bad day, the baskets were never the risk; the truck was. When it went off the road, every basket shared the fate she'd carefully diversified against.

Your funds were the baskets; the truck was what they all stood on. Funds with different names can hold overlapping companies, and in a true panic, investors sell everything at once to raise cash — correlations that were low in calm years snap to one in a crash. Diversification across assets that share a hidden common support is decoration.

What the analogy prescribes: diversify across trucks, not just baskets. That means assets that genuinely live in different places — cash (which doesn't ride in any truck), bonds of a stable government, perhaps assets in different currencies or countries — while accepting the honest limit the farmer knows: a regional drought still exists. In 2008-style weather, almost every truck is on the same flooded road. Diversification was never a promise that nothing falls; it's a way to make sure one failure isn't total. Judge it by that standard and the advice survives — narrower than the slogan, but real.
I'm choosing between two contractors. The cheaper one is booked solid for months and rushes; the pricier one has slack in his schedule. My gut says slack matters. Why?

Your gut is thinking like an engineer, so borrow their picture: bridges are not built to hold exactly the weight expected on them. A bridge designed for ten-ton trucks is built to hold far more, because the designers know the future contains a heavier truck, a flood, a mistake in the calculations — the margin of safety is the difference between the load you expect and the load that would break it. Engineers don't call that waste; they call it the reason bridges stay up.

Your rushed contractor is a bridge built to exactly its rated load. His schedule has no margin, so your project absorbs every surprise: his other job overrunning becomes your delay, a sick employee becomes your missed week, and any mistake he makes has no slack in which to fix it — so it gets papered over instead, inside your walls. The pricier contractor's empty days aren't idleness you're funding; they're the margin you're buying, the capacity to absorb the surprises your renovation will certainly produce.

The general rule travels well beyond contractors: in any plan — a budget, a deadline, a journey to the airport — ask where the margin is and what eats it. A plan with no slack isn't efficient. It's a bridge rated for exactly the truck that's coming, in a world that always sends a heavier one eventually.
A financial adviser keeps asking about my 'liquidity needs'. I own a house worth a lot. Am I not wealthy enough to stop worrying?

Think of your wealth as water in two forms. Some of it is a flowing river — cash in the bank, available this afternoon at full value. Some of it is an ice sculpture: genuinely valuable, genuinely yours, and completely unusable for paying a bill on Friday, because turning it back into water takes time and you lose some of it if you melt it in a hurry.

Your house is a magnificent ice sculpture. Its value is real, but a roof emergency, a lost job, or a tax bill arrives as a demand for river water, on the river's schedule. Selling a house takes months; borrowing against it takes weeks and a credit check at exactly the moment your finances look worst. People with large sculptures and thin rivers get forced into the worst transaction there is: melting a valuable asset at a discount because the calendar gave them no choice.

So the adviser's question, translated, is: how much of your wealth is water? Liquidity isn't about being rich or poor — it's about the match between the form your wealth is in and the timing of the demands life will make on it. Keep enough river for the emergencies, and the sculpture can stay frozen, appreciating, undisturbed.
Why is the third hour of studying so much less useful than the first? Same subject, same desk.

Because you're thirsty in the first hour and drowning in the third. Think of glasses of water when you've come in from a run: the first glass is almost life-changing, the second is good, the third is a chore, and a sixth would make you feel worse. Nothing about the water changed — what changed is how much you already had. Economists call this diminishing returns, and it applies to almost any input poured into a fixed situation.

Studying works the same way because the 'situation' — your alertness, the unlearned material within reach — depletes as you go. In hour one, you're fresh and picking up the biggest, easiest gains. By hour three you're tired, re-reading the same lines, and mostly re-encountering what you now already know. The hour didn't get worse; its marginal value fell.

The decision this analogy actually drives: stop asking 'how much studying is good?' and start asking 'what's the next hour worth compared to its alternatives?' — sleep, which consolidates memory, or exercise, or a different subject whose first-glass value is still high. Rotate inputs while each is still in its valuable early glasses, and the total day holds far more than grinding one input into its worthless sixth glass.
Our shop raised prices, which reduced sales, so we raised prices again to cover costs, and sales fell further. What's happening to us?

You've built a feedback loop, and the clearest picture of one is the squeal when a microphone gets too close to its own speaker. The microphone hears the speaker, amplifies it, the speaker plays it louder, the microphone hears that — and within a second a quiet room is screaming. Nothing new entered the system; the output became the input, and each pass amplified it.

Map your shop onto it. Higher prices (output) reduced your customer count (input to the next round). Fewer customers meant fixed costs spread over fewer sales, which pushed you to raise prices again (amplification), which cut customers further. Each individual decision looked rational — 'we must cover costs' — but the loop doesn't care about the logic of each step; it cares that the steps feed each other. A thermostat is the opposite kind of loop: its output cancels its input, which is why rooms stabilize and your shop isn't stabilizing.

Breaking a squeal never happens by singing more carefully into the microphone; you break the loop's connection — move the speaker, cut the gain. Your equivalents: cut a cost that isn't price (reduce fixed costs so the spread pressure drops), or accept lower prices deliberately to rebuild the customer count that everything else depends on. What won't work is a fourth turn of the same handle — the loop has shown you what it does with those.
Is buying a lottery ticket ever rational? Be honest with me.

Honest answer: as an investment, no; as entertainment, sometimes — and an umbrella shows you the arithmetic of why. Suppose a $2 umbrella would keep you dry, and there's a 30% chance of rain. Buying it is a bet you 'lose' 70% of the time — no rain, wasted money — and it's still sensible, because the cost is small and the bad outcome it prevents is real and likely enough to matter. Now flip it: a $2 ticket pays only if an event with odds of about 1 in 300 million happens. Multiply the prize by the probability and the ticket's expected value is a fraction of its price — as a financial instrument it's an umbrella against a rain that essentially never comes, in a desert, at a premium.

But here's the honest second half. What most buyers actually purchase isn't the jackpot; it's the few days of pleasant daydreaming between buying and the draw — 'what would I do with it' is a real experience people enjoy, and $2 for a weekend of it compares fine with $2 of any other small entertainment. The ticket becomes irrational only when it's bought as a plan: when the daydream substitutes for saving, or the spending grows past entertainment size chasing a rescue.

So the decision rule the analogy hands you: price it as a film ticket, not as a financial product. If the amount you'd spend still feels fine when you assume — correctly — that you will never win, buy it with a clear conscience. If any part of you is counting on the win, that's the umbrella budget for a rain that isn't coming, and it belongs in savings instead.
I put a holiday on my credit card. The minimum payments seem tiny. Why does everyone act like this is an emergency?

Because you've seen the snowball analogy for savings — now meet the same snowball rolling toward you. Compound interest doesn't care which side of it you're on. On a card balance, each month's interest is calculated on the whole growing pile: the holiday, plus last month's interest, plus the interest on that interest. Minimum payments are designed to barely outpace the new interest being added, which is why the pile shrinks so slowly it can feel stationary while it quietly costs you a second holiday in interest.

Do the snowball arithmetic on a typical case: $3,000 at around 24% annual interest, paying only minimums, can take the better part of a decade to clear and cost roughly another $3,000 in interest — the holiday, bought twice, with the second one invisible. The same math that makes a small pension pot impressive over thirty years makes a small balance expensive over ten.

The encouraging flip side is also in the analogy: snowballs are most sensitive early. A fixed payment noticeably above the minimum — even a modest one held constant as the balance falls — attacks the pile while it's small, and the curve bends the other way. The emergency isn't the holiday; it's letting the minimum payment choose the size of your snowball for you.
I have one free evening a week. I keep agonizing over whether to spend it on my language class or seeing friends. Is there a smarter way to think about this?

Picture a small stage with one evening's slot. Two acts want it: the language class and your friends. The crucial insight is that the slot can only be filled once — booking the class doesn't just gain you the class, it costs you the friends, automatically, whether you think about them or not. Economists call that cost the opportunity cost, and the stage makes it impossible to un-see: every 'yes' is a 'no' wearing a disguise.

The smarter question isn't 'is the class worth two hours?' — almost everything is worth two hours in isolation. It's 'is the class worth more than the best alternative use of this exact slot?' Sometimes the answer is the class, clearly. Sometimes you notice the real comparison was never class-versus-friends but class-versus-the-third-time-this-month, and the friends' act has been waiting longest.

One refinement the stage also gives you: some acts can share a bill and some can't. Friends who'd join you for a language-exchange evening collapse the trade-off entirely — worth checking before agonizing. But where the slot truly holds one act, stop asking 'is this good?' and ask 'is this the best act for this slot?' That's the whole discipline, and it applies to money and attention exactly as it applies to your Thursday.
Todo el mundo me dice que necesito un fondo de emergencia, pero mi dinero está quieto en la cuenta y me parece un desperdicio. ¿Para qué sirve exactamente?

Piensa en la rueda de repuesto de tu coche. Pesa, ocupa sitio en el maletero y, si lo piensas fríamente, es un desperdicio: llevas años conduciendo sin usarla y ese dinero podría estar en otra cosa. Pero nadie la quita para aligerar el coche, porque su valor no está en los días normales —está en un único momento: el pinchazo en la carretera, de noche, lejos de todo. En ese momento, la rueda no vale lo que costó; vale el viaje entero.

El fondo de emergencia es esa rueda. Su trabajo no es crecer ni rendir; es existir en el momento exacto en que todo lo demás falla a la vez: pierdes el empleo, se rompe la caldera, hay una urgencia familiar. Sin rueda, ese momento se paga con deuda cara o vendiendo cosas a la desesperada. Con rueda, es solo un mal mes.

La analogía también te dice el tamaño correcto: no llevas cuatro ruedas de repuesto, llevas una, adecuada para tu coche. Traducido: unos meses de gastos esenciales, ni más ni menos. Y cuando por fin la usas, la prioridad siguiente no es invertir ni gastar: es volver a poner una rueda en el maletero. El dinero 'quieto' no está desperdiciado; está de guardia.
Why do refundable plane tickets cost so much more than non-refundable ones? The seat is the same.

Because you're not buying the same thing — you're buying the seat plus a door left open. Think of it as renting a hall. A non-refundable booking is cheaper because you've handed the owner certainty: that date is sold, full stop, and he can plan around it. The refundable booking costs more because you've kept an option: the right to walk away at the last minute and leave him with an empty hall he can no longer sell. Options are never free, because the other party carries the risk you declined.

Once you see it, you see it everywhere: the flexible hotel rate, the returnable appliance, the contract with a break clause, the job offer you keep warm while deciding. In each case the premium is the price of not deciding yet — of keeping future choices alive while information improves.

That gives you the decision rule. The premium is worth paying when the future is genuinely uncertain and the cost of being locked in is high: a trip that depends on a visa, a project that may be cancelled. It's wasted when your plans are as certain as plans get — then you're buying a door you will never open, and the non-refundable fare is the same seat at the honest price. Price flexibility as what it is — insurance against your own change of mind — and buy exactly as much of it as your uncertainty justifies.
Why does paying someone by the hour versus by the job change how they work? Same person, same task.

Because you've changed what you're buying, and people — quite rationally — sell you exactly that. Picture hiring a mover. By the hour, you are buying his time: every extra trip, every careful pause, every slow elevator ride is money to him, and the meter rewards thoroughness and punishes hurry. By the job, you are buying a finished move: now speed is his profit, and the same care that was diligence an hour ago is now costing him money — the incentive points at the corners, and corners get cut.

Neither mover is dishonest; each is responding precisely to the meter you installed. Economists call this the principal-agent problem — the person acting (agent) has different information and, unless you design carefully, different interests than the person paying (principal) — but the mover shows you the whole mechanism without the vocabulary: you don't get what you want, you get what you measure and pay for.

The decision skill is choosing the meter to match what you actually value and can verify. Pay by the job when the result is easy to inspect at the end (a painted wall, a moved piano). Pay by the hour when the process matters and can't be checked afterward (care, judgment, advice) — and when you can't verify either, expect the gap between your interest and theirs to be filled by reputation and repeat business, which is why the mover your neighbors rehire behaves like neither extreme.
Small habits are supposed to matter over time, but honestly, one skipped workout or one coffee a day feels like nothing. Convince me or tell me I'm right.

You're right about the single event and wrong about the sum, and a flight shows both halves. A plane flying from one city to another that is off course by a single degree — an error so small the passengers can't feel it — doesn't arrive slightly wrong. One degree, sustained over hundreds of kilometers, puts it over a completely different city. The error didn't grow; it accumulated, because every kilometer of travel carried the small angle forward and added distance to it.

Your coffee and your workout are angles, not events. One coffee is genuinely nothing; the habit is the same small amount repeated along a long route — hundreds of coffees, thousands in money, a measurable angle on your finances. The skipped workout matters only the same way: not as a lost day, but as a slight change in heading for your fitness, repeated until the destination is visibly different.

The analogy also tells you where the argument stops, which slogans don't: a plane can correct its heading at any point, and the correction is worth most early, when the remaining distance is longest. That's the actual reason to care about small habits — not guilt over one coffee, but the cheapness of a one-degree correction now versus the expensive one later. Skip the coffee or don't; just don't mistake 'each step is tiny' for 'the direction doesn't matter'.
Teach me fractions properly. The pizza thing got me through school but I still freeze when it's not food — like 'what is 2/3 of 90?'

Let's use the pizza one last time, then take it away. Two-thirds of a pizza: cut the pizza into 3 equal slices, take 2 of them. The two numbers have jobs: the bottom number (denominator) says how many equal pieces the whole was cut into; the top number (numerator) says how many of those pieces you're taking. That's the whole idea — fractions aren't about pizza, they're about cut-and-take.

Now remove the pizza. '2/3 of 90' means: cut 90 into 3 equal parts (90 ÷ 3 = 30), then take 2 of those parts (2 × 30 = 60). No food anywhere, and it works on anything divisible: 2/3 of a rope, of a budget, of an hour (cut 60 minutes into 3 parts of 20, take 2: 40 minutes).

Here's the idea standing on its own, no analogy left: a fraction a/b of a quantity means divide the quantity by b, then multiply by a. The pizza was only ever a delivery vehicle for 'divide by the bottom, multiply by the top'. When a fraction freezes you, don't picture food — say the jobs of the two numbers out loud: cut into how many? take how many? The rest is arithmetic.
Les nombres négatifs me perdent. Moins cinq, moins moins trois... Explique-moi simplement, mais pas avec des dessins d'enfant.

Commençons par le thermomètre, puis nous le rangerons. Cinq degrés, c'est 5. Zéro, c'est le point de repère — ni chaud ni froid, juste la frontière convenue. Moins cinq, c'est 5 degrés de l'autre côté de la frontière. Le signe moins ne dit pas 'une quantité étrange' : il dit 'de l'autre côté du zéro, à cette distance'. Retenez cette phrase, elle suffit.

Maintenant, enlevons le thermomètre et gardons seulement la droite des nombres : une ligne, un zéro au milieu, les positifs d'un côté, les négatifs de l'autre, symétriques. Ajouter, c'est se déplacer ; soustraire, c'est se déplacer dans l'autre sens. Retirer un nombre négatif — le fameux 'moins moins' — revient à retirer un déplacement vers la gauche, ce qui vous fait aller vers la droite : soustraire −3, c'est donc ajouter 3. Ce n'est pas un mystère, c'est la géométrie de la ligne.

La définition qui reste quand l'image s'efface : les nombres négatifs sont les symétriques des positifs par rapport à zéro, et chaque opération est un déplacement sur la droite. Le thermomètre vous a donné l'intuition de 'l'autre côté' ; la droite vous donne les règles, y compris là où le thermomètre ne va plus — on ne peut pas avoir une température de −3 multipliée par −2, mais sur la droite, le calcul continue sans elle.
What is a function, in math? The vending machine explanation is all I've got and my course has moved past it.

Good — the vending machine got you exactly as far as it can, so let's name what it taught you and then leave it behind. In the machine: you press B3 (input), you get the crisps (output), and the same button always gives the same item. A machine that gave crisps on Monday and chocolate on Tuesday for the same button wouldn't be a vending machine you'd trust — and that reliability, 'same input, same output, every time', is the soul of the function idea.

Now the restatement, in the concept's own terms. A function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. Written f(x) = x², it says: whatever number x arrives, the output is its square. The machine disappears and three things remain that it could never show you: the rule works for infinitely many inputs, not twelve snack slots; the output can feed another function's input, machines all the way down; and 'exactly one output' is a real restriction — a rule that assigns two outputs to one input isn't a broken function, it isn't one at all.

Test yourself without the machine: is 'the square root of x' a function? Only once you specify which root — because the machine rule, 'exactly one', survives the analogy's removal and does the deciding for you.
I learned voltage and current through the water-in-pipes analogy. Now I want the version without the pipes.

Let's retire the plumbing respectfully — it gave you 'pressure' and 'flow' — and rebuild both ideas in their own terms.

Current first, because it's the more literal one: current is simply a count of how much electric charge passes a point per second. Not a substance flowing like water — a rate of passage, measured in amperes, where one ampere is a specific, enormous number of electrons drifting past per second. Notice the word drifting: the electrons themselves move at a crawl; what you care about is the count, not their journey.

Voltage is subtler, and the pipes never really had it. Voltage is a difference in electric potential energy between two points — how much energy each unit of charge gains or loses moving from one to the other. It is always a difference, always between two points; a single point cannot 'have' a voltage any more than a single point can have a height difference. That's why circuit diagrams mark voltages across components, and why the bird standing on one high-voltage wire is unharmed: both feet at the same potential, no difference, no drive for charge to move through it.

What remains when the pipes are gone: charge flows when a potential difference drives it, resistance is whatever opposes that flow, and Ohm's law relates the three. You may find you no longer miss the water — it was carrying two ideas that turn out to be a count and a difference.
Evolution was explained to me through dog breeding — humans choosing traits. But nature has no breeder. How do I think about it without one?

The breeding analogy is a good servant and a bad master, so let's use it once and dismiss it. It taught you the core transaction: if some individuals, because of their traits, leave more offspring than others, the next generation shifts toward those traits. In breeding, the choosing is done by a human with a goal. Your question is the right one: what does the choosing when nobody's home?

Remove the breeder by replacing him with circumstances. A drought doesn't choose the drought-resistant plants the way a breeder chooses a puppy — it simply is the condition in which resistant plants happen to set more seed. A new predator doesn't select for speed on purpose; slow prey get eaten, which is selection with no selector. The environment isn't an agent making decisions; it's a filter that different variants pass through at different rates.

Stated without any analogy at all: evolution is what happens when three things coexist — variation among individuals, heredity of that variation, and differing reproductive success linked to it. Given those, change over generations isn't a hypothesis, it's arithmetic. The breeder was only ever a way to make 'differing reproductive success' visible. Whenever the analogy whispers 'but who wanted this trait?', that's the breeder talking after his dismissal — traits aren't wanted; they're what the filter happened to pass.
What does 'slope' mean beyond 'steepness of a hill'? My algebra course keeps using it on graphs that aren't hills.

The hill gave you the seed of it: some hills are gentle, some are brutal, and your legs can rank them. On the hill, steepness compares two things — how much height you gain against how much ground you cover. A path that climbs 10 meters over 100 meters of walking is gentler than one that climbs the same 10 meters over 20. Hold onto that comparison; it's the entire concept. The hill itself is about to be dismissed.

Slope, standing alone: for any line, slope is the ratio of vertical change to horizontal change between two points — rise over run. y = 2x + 1 has slope 2 because every step of 1 to the right lifts the value by 2. And now the parts the hill could never show you: a line going downhill to the right has negative slope — the 'rise' is a fall — and a horizontal line has slope zero, and a vertical line has no defined slope at all, because the run is zero and the ratio collapses.

The payoff for removing the hill: slope turns out to be the general idea of a rate. Speed is the slope of distance against time; a price increase is the slope of cost against quantity. You weren't learning about hills in algebra — hills were the first rate you ever met, dressed in walking boots.
When the forecast says '70% chance of rain', what is it actually claiming? I want the real meaning, not a metaphor.

Then let's pass through the metaphor quickly and out the other side. The friendly version: imagine 100 days exactly like today — same patterns, same fronts — and on about 70 of them, it rains where you are. Umbrellas on 70 days out of 100. That's the intuition, and it's a good one.

Now remove the imaginary days and keep the precise claim. A probability of 70% is a statement about a reference class and a long run: among all situations the forecast model judges equivalent to this one, rain occurred in roughly 70% of them historically — and the forecaster is asserting today belongs to that class. Two consequences follow that the metaphor hides. First, the claim can be well-calibrated even when it doesn't rain today: a single dry day no more refutes it than one honest coin landing heads refutes fairness. Second, it says nothing about your street at your hour with certainty — it's a frequency over a class, applied to a single case.

The definition that survives: probability is the long-run relative frequency of an outcome in repeated equivalent trials — and 'it will probably rain' is you borrowing that frequency to make today's decision. The umbrella choice, by the way, needs no more precision than the metaphor gave you. Knowing what the number means is for the days when someone argues from one dry afternoon that forecasts are worthless.
Chemical equilibrium: I pictured two rooms with people wandering between them. Is that the real idea or just a picture?

It's a picture of the real idea, and a better one than most — so let's walk through it and then walk out of it. Two rooms, a doorway, people drifting both ways at random. At first everyone is in room A, so traffic flows mostly A to B. As B fills, the flow back grows. Eventually the numbers in each room stop changing — not because people stopped moving, but because the flows are equal: as many cross each way per minute. That's equilibrium, and the picture's best lesson is that it's dynamic, not frozen.

Now the chemistry in its own clothes. In a reversible reaction, molecules convert forward and backward continuously. Equilibrium is the state where the forward rate equals the reverse rate, so concentrations hold steady while reactions continue in both directions. And here the rooms mislead if you keep them: people drift at rates that depend only on headcounts in a simple way, and there's no reason the rooms must end up equal — likewise, equilibrium does not mean equal amounts of reactants and products. It means equal rates. Many equilibria sit far to one side: a room with ninety people and a room with ten can be in perfect equilibrium if the doorway flows match.

Keep the doorway for 'dynamic, balanced flows'. Discard it for 'equal shares' — the definition that remains is about rates, and it predicts things the picture can't, like how temperature shifts the balance.
Supply and demand was taught to me with an auction. What's the version of the idea that doesn't need the auctioneer?

The auction did one job for you: it made price discovery visible — you watched bids climb until buyers thinned out. Everything real in the idea survives the auctioneer's departure, so let's state it plainly.

At any given price, some quantity of a good is what buyers are willing and able to purchase, and some quantity is what sellers are willing and able to offer. These are schedules, not single numbers: lower the price and the quantity buyers want grows; raise it and the quantity sellers offer grows. Where the two schedules cross, the market clears — everyone who wants to trade at that price can. If the price sits above the crossing, unsold goods pile up and sellers shade prices down; below it, queues form and prices get bid up. The 'auction' you pictured is just this adjustment happening loudly, in one room, in one afternoon.

What the restated version gives you that the gavel couldn't: an explanation of prices that never saw an auction — rent, wages, the cost of a haircut. Nobody bids openly for those; the schedules still cross, and shortages and gluts still push prices toward the crossing, just quietly and slowly. The auction was training wheels on a bicycle that turns out to be most of economic life.
Derivatives were introduced to me as 'the speedometer of a function'. I need to know what one actually is now.

The speedometer earned its place: a car's odometer tells you where you've been in total, the speedometer tells you how fast that's changing right now, and the difference between 'total' and 'right now' is the entire doorway into calculus. Walk through it and let's put the car away.

Start with average rate, which needs no analogy: between hour 1 and hour 3, a quantity grew from 10 to 22 — an average rate of 6 per hour. Now shrink the window: between hour 2.9 and 3.0, between 2.99 and 3.00. As the window closes toward zero, the average rate settles toward a specific value — the rate at the instant itself. The derivative is that limiting value: the slope of the curve at a single point, defined as the limit of average slopes over shrinking intervals.

What the definition gives you that the dashboard never could: it works on anything that changes — temperature, population, profit — and it can be computed from a formula, exactly, rather than read off a dial approximately. And the speedometer had a hidden cheat: the car's computer itself estimates from tiny intervals. The derivative is the value those estimates approach. Keep the intuition — 'how fast, right now' — and let the limit be the meaning.
Explain quantum superposition with an everyday analogy. A coin spinning? A cat? I need something I can picture.

I'm going to decline the analogy — not to be difficult, but because here the analogy is the main source of the misunderstanding, and you'd leave with a picture that feels like knowledge and isn't.

Watch what the usual candidates smuggle in. A spinning coin suggests the particle is really heads or really tails at each instant, just changing too fast to see — but experiments rule exactly that out: the outcomes can't be explained by the particle having a definite state all along. The cat suggests a weird mixture of two ordinary states, which imports a macroscopic absurdity the physics never claimed and invites you to argue with the picture instead of the theory. Every household object obeys the rule 'it is in one definite state, even if unknown' — and superposition is precisely the failure of that rule. An analogy built from things that obey the rule cannot carry a concept defined by breaking it.

So here is the honest, analogy-free version. Before measurement, a quantum system is described by a mathematical object that assigns amplitudes to possible outcomes; the probabilities of outcomes come from those amplitudes, and — the crucial, unpicturable part — amplitudes can cancel or reinforce each other, which is why quantum behavior shows interference patterns no 'unknown definite state' can produce. On measurement, you get one outcome, with those probabilities. That paragraph is less satisfying than a spinning coin. It's also true, and the coin isn't. Some ideas have to be met on their own ground, with the mathematics as the only ladder — this is the famous one.
Infinity — I keep picturing it as an enormous number at the end of the number line. Fix my picture with a better one.

The fix isn't a better picture — it's removing the picture, because the 'enormous number at the end' image is itself the error, and the popular replacement, the infinite hotel, often makes it worse: it leaves people thinking infinity is a very large quantity that behaves oddly, rather than not a quantity at all.

Start from the definition, which is genuinely simple. A process or collection is infinite if it has no end — full stop. The counting numbers are infinite not because they reach some colossal final number, but because for every number you name, the rule 'add one' produces another. There is no last guest in the hotel because there is no last room, not because the hotel is huge. Size language — bigger, enormous, at the end — is the analogy smuggling itself back in.

This is why infinity breaks ordinary arithmetic intuitions: half of the counting numbers (the even ones) can be matched one-to-one with all of them, which is absurd for any finite collection and unremarkable once 'infinite' means 'endless' rather than 'maximal'. If a picture is forced on you, take the horizon rather than a distant mountain: walking toward it is real, arriving is a category error. But the definition is shorter than any image: no end. Everything true about infinity is bookkeeping on those two words.
A study says p < 0.05. A friend explained it as 'like a courtroom: the effect is guilty beyond reasonable doubt.' Is that right?

Your friend's analogy is popular and it will lead you astray, so let's not use it. The courtroom imports two falsehoods: that there is a defendant whose guilt is being established (a p-value never measures the probability that an effect is real), and that a threshold verdict settles the matter (science doesn't acquit hypotheses). Reasoning from it, people conclude p < 0.05 means '95% chance the result is true' — the single most common misreading of statistics, and the analogy manufactures it.

Here is the definition, plainly, with no courtroom. Assume, for argument, that there is no effect at all — the drug does nothing, the coin is fair. The p-value is the probability that pure chance alone would produce data at least as extreme as what was observed. p = 0.03 says: in a world where nothing is going on, results this striking would show up about 3 times in 100 repetitions. That's all. It's a statement about the data given a boring world — not a statement about the probability that the world is boring, which is what everyone wants and what the number does not contain.

Used correctly, it's a filter with known behavior: if you run many tests on nothing, about 5 in 100 will pass p < 0.05 by luck — which is why one small study is a lead, not a verdict, and why replication exists. No analogy carries those three facts without bending one of them; the definition, memorized once, carries all three.
Ha muerto el perro de mi hijo, que tiene seis años. Pensaba decirle que se fue a dormir y que está en un lugar mejor, para que no sufra. ¿Es buena idea?

Es una idea que nace del cariño, pero no te la recomiendo, y la razón es que las analogías con un niño no son decoración: son el material con el que construye su comprensión, y esta en concreto le enseña cosas falsas que tendrá que desaprender con miedo.

Si el perro 'se fue a dormir', dormir se convierte en algo peligroso: hay niños que empiezan a temer la hora de acostarse, o que esperan cada mañana que el perro despierte. Si 'está en un lugar mejor' sin más explicación, el niño puede preguntarse por qué no puede ir a visitarlo, o por qué el perro prefirió ese lugar a estar con él. La metáfora intenta evitar una conversación y crea tres.

Lo que funciona mejor es la verdad en palabras de su tamaño, sin analogía: 'Su cuerpo dejó de funcionar y murió. No va a volver, y no es culpa de nadie. Estamos tristes porque lo queríamos mucho, y está bien estar triste.' Los niños toleran la realidad directa mejor que los adultos; lo que les desestabiliza es la incoherencia entre lo que se les dice y lo que perciben —y perciben tu tristeza con total claridad—. Puedes ofrecerle un ritual real en lugar de una ficción: enterrar al perro, dibujarlo, contar historias de él. El consuelo no necesita un disfraz; necesita hechos suaves y un adulto que se quede al lado mientras duelen.
Give me an analogy for consciousness. Like, the brain is hardware and the mind is the software running on it — something like that?

That particular analogy is exactly the one to refuse, because it doesn't explain consciousness — it quietly decides the argument about it in advance, and you deserve to see the trick before adopting it.

Watch what 'hardware and software' smuggles in. Software is separable from hardware: the same program runs on different machines, can be copied, paused, and inspected from outside. If the mind is the brain's software, then minds should be copyable, transferable, and independent of their particular wet hardware — conclusions that are fiercely disputed open questions in philosophy and neuroscience, not established facts. The analogy doesn't argue for them; it assumes them and then presents the assumption as an explanation. Other popular candidates cheat differently: 'the mind is what the brain does' is a claim, not an analogy; the 'ghost in the machine' framing rigs the game in the opposite direction.

The honest position is shorter and less satisfying: we can describe correlations between brain states and experience in growing detail, we can say a great deal about what consciousness does — attention, report, integration — and the question of why any of it is accompanied by subjective experience at all remains genuinely open. When every available analogy is a conclusion wearing a costume, the correct move is to state the state of knowledge directly and leave the space where the analogy would go respectfully empty. Not every gap in our understanding is improved by filling it with furniture from another room.
My lease has a clause about 'quiet enjoyment'. My friend says it's basically like a promise the landlord won't bother me. Can I rely on that reading?

Don't rely on the analogy — this is a case where the friendly paraphrase can cost you money, because 'quiet enjoyment' is a legal term of art, and its legal meaning is both narrower and stranger than the everyday promise it resembles. Your friend's version suggests a general pledge of non-interference. The clause in law concerns the landlord's own actions substantially interfering with your use of the property — things like cutting off essential services, changing locks, or entering without proper notice — and it has been shaped by centuries of cases into specific shapes that 'won't bother me' doesn't capture. Some serious annoyances fall outside it; some landlord actions you'd never describe as 'bothering' fall inside.

The general principle is worth keeping: when words appear in a contract, a statute, or a diagnosis, they may be terms of art — cargo from a technical system — and an everyday analogy translates them into a language where their precise edges are lost. Those edges are exactly what disputes are about. Nobody reads a lease for the gist; the gist is what you had before the document existed.

So the right move here is unglamorous: read the clause itself, check what your jurisdiction's tenancy guidance says the term covers, and if real money or your home is at stake, spend an hour with a lawyer rather than an analogy. Analogies are for understanding ideas. Contracts are enforced as texts.
My friend's mother just died. I want to comfort her by saying I understand — it's like when my grandfather died. Should I say it that way?

Keep the grandfather out of the sentence — not because your grief wasn't real, but because the comparison does the opposite of what you intend. 'It's like when my grandfather died' asks her, in the worst week of her life, to do translation work: to map her loss onto yours, find them similar, and feel accompanied. What she usually hears instead is that the conversation has quietly moved to your experience, and that hers has been filed under a category. Grief is the subject where analogy most reliably fails, because the thing being grieved is precisely the part that isn't like anything else — this mother, this relationship, this absence.

What works instead is direct and unadorned, and it's shorter than any analogy: 'I'm so sorry. I loved hearing about her. I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere.' If you want your own experience present, offer it as availability rather than equivalence — 'I lost my grandfather a few years ago; if it ever helps to talk to someone who's been through a version of it, I'm here' — and then let her decide whether the comparison gets made. The difference looks small on paper. In the room, it's the difference between being accompanied and being explained to.

The general rule: analogies are for ideas, where being approximately right is useful. For pain, approximation is the injury. Say the true, specific thing, or say the simple thing — but don't hand someone a metaphor to hold when what they needed was you.
Is time just a fourth dimension, like the three dimensions of space but one more? That's how it's always drawn for me.

The drawing is doing you a disservice, and this is a case where it's better to state the asymmetry directly than to find a friendlier picture. The claim 'time is the fourth dimension' is mathematically real — relativity genuinely unifies space and time into a four-dimensional spacetime, and the equations treat them together. But every analogy from spatial dimensions smuggles in the one property that matters most and that time does not have: freedom of movement.

In space, you can move in any direction, reverse, stand still, revisit a place. A dimension, in the everyday picture, is an axis you're free to travel. In time you can do none of these things: you move in one direction, at a rate you can influence only slightly and only in comparison to others (relativity does allow clocks to disagree — but never to run backward, and never to stop). Inside the mathematics this asymmetry is visible: time enters the spacetime interval with the opposite sign to the spatial dimensions, which is the formal way of saying it is not 'space, but more of it'. The light-cone structure — the division of everything into reachable future, reachable past, and the unreachable elsewhere — has no spatial counterpart at all.

So the accurate statement, without analogy: spacetime is four-dimensional, and one of its dimensions differs from the other three in sign, in causal structure, and in your ability to traverse it. 'Just another dimension' papers over precisely the differences that make time time. Some analogies fail because they're inaccurate in detail; this one fails because it's inaccurate in essence — and those are the ones to retire completely rather than repair.
